topics.title: Chapter overview
topics.summary: Data-oriented design begins with transformations and access patterns. Harbor processes active measurements repeatedly, so it can build a dense active-value sequence once and operate on that sequence instead of repeatedly chasing objects and checking the same state. The chapter compares representations without claiming that object-oriented and data-oriented design are mutually exclusive ideologies.

topics.title: 18.1.1 Grouping Frequently Processed Data
topics.summary: Identify which fields are read together, which are written together, and how often each transformation runs. Grouping data by that workload can reduce irrelevant memory traffic and simplify loops. A dense active set may be useful when many passes operate on a relatively stable subset.

topics.title: 18.1.2 Eliminating Pointer-Chasing Structures
topics.summary: Indirection can express flexible relationships, but each pointer load may delay discovery of the next address. Contiguous indices or compact arrays can make traversal more predictable and easier to batch. Replacing pointers also changes lifetime and identity management, which must be designed explicitly.

topics.title: 18.2.1 Evaluating Abstraction Costs
topics.summary: An abstraction’s cost depends on its implementation and use. A small value type can compile to efficient contiguous operations, while an apparently low-level pointer graph can have poor locality. Virtual dispatch, allocation, and indirection are measurable mechanisms, not inevitable properties of every class.

topics.title: Trace the implementation
topics.summary: ActiveSnapshot owns a materialized copy of the selected values. It does not borrow pointers into the entity vector, so later entity mutation cannot silently change the snapshot. The test makes that behavior explicit by activating a previously inactive entity and verifying that only a newly built snapshot includes it.
